title: Area Code Finder: US Codes by State
description: Find which area codes serve a US state with the Area Code Finder — NANP codes, overlays and the context behind them. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a number beginning 212 is Manhattan's famous original code — today sharing the island with overlay codes the Finder lists beside it.
quick_answer: The Area Code Finder lists the area codes that serve a US state, with the location context around them. Choose the state or search the context and read its codes — including the overlays that mean a single city can answer to several codes at once.
steps_intro: Area codes are geography wearing numbers. Read the state's set:

body.t: A caller's code hints at their state — with the portability caveat below. The Finder supplies the hint; judgement supplies the rest.
A local presence starts with the right code. See the state's full set, overlays included, before choosing.
Phone columns with impossible state-code pairings expose themselves against this list — one of data hygiene's cheapest checks.
Why does one state have one code and California dozens? Population, history and overlays — the Finder's context answers while it lists.

212 (Manhattan), 213 (Los Angeles) and 312 (Chicago) date from the original 1947 NANP assignments — small codes for the biggest cities, because rotary dials made low digits faster. Their states' modern lists run much longer.
A growing metro exhausts its code and gains an overlay: two codes, one geography, ten-digit dialling for everyone. The Finder lists both because both are true.

popular_table.note: Area codes are NANP (North American Numbering Plan) geography — the US, Canada and parts of the Caribbean share the +1 system the Finder works within.

faq: Outside the US?
The NANP covers Canada and some Caribbean nations under +1; this Finder's state framing is US-first. Other countries use entirely different dialling geographies.
One code, one city?
No — codes serve regions, and overlays stack several on one city. A code narrows a number to an area, never (by itself) to a street.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — you choose the state; nothing about your own location is involved.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Numbering geography and map geography are maintained by different bodies on different clocks; both are right in their own frame.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No — and this tool never asks for it.
Does a code prove where a caller lives?
No — mobile numbers move with their owners. A code says where the number was born, which is a hint, not an address.
Why do new codes look random?
The elegant low-digit codes went first (1947). New assignments draw from what remains — history you can hear in the digits.
Why does my state list begin with low numbers?
Early assignments favoured low digits for big cities (rotary dials). The list's archaeology is visible in its first entries.
Are toll-free codes in the list?
800-family codes are geography-free by design, so they are not a state's codes. The Finder lists geographic NANP codes.
A code on the list serves another state too.
A few historical codes straddle borders. The Finder reports the state's relationship honestly rather than forcing exclusivity.
